course.title: Pancreas
course.html:
Anatomy

  • Digestive (exocrine) and hormonal (endocrine) functions
  • Positioned at transpyloric plane (L1) → epigastrium and left hypochondrium regions
  • With exception of tail → retroperitoneal organ
  • Stomach – Separated from pancreas by lesser sac, stomach and pylorus lie anterior
  • Duodenum – D1 lies anteriorly, D2 lies laterally to pancreatic head
  • Transverse mesocolon – Attaches to anterior surface of pancreas
  • Common bile duct – Descends behind head before opening into major pancreatic duct
  • Spleen – located posteriorly and laterally
  • Aorta and IVC pass posteriorly to head
  • Superior mesenteric vessels lie behind neck and anterior to uncinate process → come anterior over D3
  • Posterior to neck → splenic and superior mesenteric veins unite to portal vein
  • Splenic artery traverses superior border of pancreas
  • Composed of head, uncinate process, neck, body, tail
  • Tail lies within close proximity to hilum of spleen
  • Exocrine pancreas: acini → intercalated ducts →
  • intralobular collecting ducts → main pancreatic duct (Wirsung duct) → unites with common bile duct = hepatopancreatic duct → opens into ampulla of Vater and into duodenum via major duodenal papilla
  • Secretions controlled by sphincter of Oddi
  • Arterial supply: splenic artery, head also by superior and inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries (branches of gastroduodenal and superior mesenteric arteries)
  • Venous drainage: speenic vein, head drained into superior mesenteric branches of hepatic portal vein
  • Lymphatic vessels: follow arterial supply, empty into pancreaticosplenal nodes and pyloric nodes, then into

superior mesenteric and coeliac lymph nodes

Benign pancreatic disorders

Acute pancreatitis

= inflammatory process of pancreas with variable involvement of other regional tissues or remote organ systems

  • Mild and severe forms
  • In mild acute pancreatitis → only edema of retroperitoneal area, involving especially peripancreatic tissue
  • organ dysfunction is minimal and recovery without sequelae
  • In severe acute pancreatitis → pancreatic and retroperitoneal fat necrosis with involvement of remote structures

(e.g., mesentery) + complications (ascites, haemorrhage, septic shock) and organ failure (first week)

  • Overall mortality - 15%, but rises to 30% in severe AP

Pathophysiology

Trypsinogen = first proenzyme to be activated in duodenum

  • Protective mechanisms against excessive or premature activation
  • high levels of trypsin inhibit pancreatic secretion
  • separate packing of proenzymes into zymogen vesicles
  • combination of zymogen with protease inhibitors
  • Abnormal activation started by lysosomes → activate trypsinogen in zymogen capsules → activated enzymes get in extracellular space → positive chemotactism for neutrophils and macrophages → aggravate inflammation
  • Local edema
  • Elastase damages vascular wall → hemorrhage and necrosis
  • Systemic inflammation mediators → respiratory and renal complications, even death

Etiology

  • I GET SMASHED
  • Gallstones migrating into CBD and irritating sphincter of Oddi (1/3 of cases)
  • Microstones and cholesterolosis easily pass through cystic duct and Oddi
  • Alcohol (1/3)
  • ERCP (1-3%)
  • Injecting iodinated contrast can raise intraductal pressure enough to start enzymatic cascade
  • Hypertriglyceridemia
  • Abdominal blunt trauma (bicycle, hoof, tire explosion) crush pancreas against spine
  • Drug-induced pancreatitis is usually mild → azathioprine, sulfonamides, tetracyclines, valproic acid, estrogens,

furosemide, 5-ASA’s, corticosteroids, octreotide

  • Most common infection → mumps
  • Post-OP or iatrogenic AP
  • Hypercalcemia, hyperparathyroidism, toxic doses of vit. D
  • Idiopathic

Signs and symptoms

  • Abdominal pain → severe, upper half of abdomen, increasing intensity, posterior radiation, duration of several days
  • Fever during first days caused by inflammation (not infection)
  • High fever after 2 weeks due to infection of necrotic area
  • Hypotension and tachycardia
  • Absence of bowel movements, passing stool and gas (paralytic ileus; guarding)
  • Nausea and vomiting

Physical exam

  • Can mimic peptic ulcer or peritonitis (intense pain, tenderness, guarding and rebound tenderness (Blumberg sign))
  • DD = negative DRE
  • Early ascites in severe forms
  • Absent bowl sounds and abd. distension due to paralytic ileus
  • Grey Turner sign
  • Cullen’s sign
  • Jaundice (biliary AP)
  • Dyspnea in case of subphrenic collections irritating diaphragm, pleural effusion or ARDS
  • Subcutaneous fat necrosis due to circulating lipase → erythematous nodules

+ Funduscopic examination of eyes → ischemic injury in severe cases; can lead to blindness

+ Uncoherence by aggression of phospholypase A on sphingomielines of nervous system

DD → acute abdomen

Need emergency surgeryAcute non-surgical abdomen
- Cholecystitis
- Cholangitis
- Duodenal or gastric perforated ulcer
- Colonic Obstruction
- Mesenteric infarction
- Ectopic pregnancy		- Myocardial infarction
- Bacterial pneumonia
- Reno-uretheral colic

Lab

1. Serum amylase and lipase- 3-10x higher than normal
- Lipase is more useful due to its longer T ½ (not routinely)
2.Trypsin, trypsinogen, trypsinogen- Not routinely
activation peptide
3. Cholestasis markers (ALP, total bilirubin)- Can indicate gallstone
and cytolysis enzymes (AST, ALT)
4. Cholesterol and TG’s
5. Calcium5. Calcium- Hypocalcemia secondary to binding of Ca2+ to fatty acids
resulting from saponification of fat
- Rarely hypercalcemia as cause
6. Glucose
7. WBC7. WBC- Usually elevated → initially due to inflammation and after at
least one week due to infection of necrotic tissue
8. Hct- Usually high at admission because of edema and ascites
- It may then drop in severe cases due to necrotic-hemorrhagic
lesions
9. CRP !!!- > 10 mg/dL at 48 hours after onset is prognostic factor for organ
failure
- CRP is not specific for pancreatitis
10. Electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen,
creatinine, arterial blood
gases must be followed to diagnose any
renal or respiratory problems

Imaging

Plain X-ray- Not very useful, but can show
→ Pneumoperitoneum due to hollow organ perforation (DD)
→ Paralytic ileus
→ Sentinel loop sign = dilatation of first jejunal loop
→ Colon cut off sign = associates dilation of transverse colon with empty gas left flexure
→ Calcification in pancreatic area (stigmata of CP)
Abdominal US- Limited help because of ileus
- Technique of choice for detecting gallbladder lithiasis
- Not reliable for CBD stones
Abdominal CT= best imaging method
→ Balthazar grading scale is based on CT findings
A = normal
B = enlargement
C = peripancreatic inflammation
D = single fluid collection
E = multiple fluid collections
→ Risk of infection and mortality - none for A and B; rises from C to E
CT (or US) guided needle aspiration → important to asses infection of necrosis
ERCP- Used with caution in biliary AP in first 3 days from onset; later risk of aggravation
MRCP- Offers comparable result to ERCP – without risks !
Endoscopic US- Better data than plain US + biopsy → DD

Prognosis

  • Ranson score → calculated only first 48 hours after onset
    • Each one gives 1 point
    • Mortality rises at 50% for score > 5

WBC

8 mg/dl

Complications

1. Pseudocyst= collection of pancreatic fluid and necrotic debris enclosed by
neighboring organs; without walls
- Pseudocysto-jejunostomy on Y loop = technique of choice
→ Better than stomach/ duodenum because no food can get into it
- Transpapillary drainage
- Percutaneous drainage
- Transmural drainage
2. Pancreatic abscess and
infected necrosis		- Caused by bacteria from intestinal flora
- Laparoscopic removal (3-4 weeks after onset is best moment)
- CT guided needle aspiration
3. Pancreatic duct disruption- Associated with extensive pancreatic necrosis
- If drainage is in place → discharges very high amylase levels
- Transpapillary stent can be useful
- Can communicate with pseudocyst
- Can cause fistulas → have fibrotic tract → fistulo-jejunostomy on Y
loop should be performed
4. Hemorrhage- Rare
- Due to elastase

Treatment

  • Fluid resuscitation without waiting for lab values (ascites and edema cause severe fluid loss)
  • In order to have exact fluid balance → bladder catheter and gastric aspiration
  • Central venous and arterial line mandatory in pat. with poor status
  • No oral intake allowed → ileus
  • Avoidance of morphine → spastic of Oddi s. → choose other analgesics !
  • AB (meropenem/ imipenem) for 14 days or longer if systemic complications occur
  • Antifungal prophylaxis → fluconazole
  • Octreotide may improve outcome
  • Hemodiafiltration (CHDF) on polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) membranes helps in eliminating cytokines
  • Selective digestive decontamination (SDD) but only in selected patients
  • Total parenteral nutrition not routinely recommended
  • Endoscopically assisted naso-jejunal feeding tube or surgical jejunostomy preferred
  • Surgery
  • It has to be avoided first 2 weeks
  • Sterile necrosis has to be treated in conservative manner
  • Sterile necrosis can benefit from surgery if there is tendency to extension or in fulminant AP (organ failure at less

than 72 from onset)

  • Infection of necrotic pancreatic or peripancreatic tissue has to be operated
  • Technique must evacuate necrosis but has to spare as much tissue as possible
  • Cholecystectomy is mandatory in every gallstone AP or even idiopathic AP to avoid recurrence
  • Minimally invasive approach has to be limited to highly specialized centers
  • Laparostomy (peritoneal cavity is opened anteriorly and deliberately left open) with necrosectomy + lavage

(can be repeated as often as possible)

  • Closed lavage possible but not often used
  • Vac-pac indicated in SAP with abdominal hypertension and compartment syndrome
  • Other method - retroperitoneoscopy

Chronic pancreatitis

= continuing inflammatory pathology of pancreas leading to irreversible morphologic changes which causes exocrine and endocrine pancreatic insufficiency

Etiology

  • TIGAR-O classification system
Toxic and metabolic factors- Alcohol !! (70%)
- Tobacco
Idiopathic
Genetic predisposition
Autoimmune- Isolated autoimmune pancreatitis
- Chronic pancreatitis associated with other autoimmune diseases
(Sjorgen syndrome, scleroderma, PSC, primary biliary cirrhosis)
Recurrence of severe AP- After necrosis
- Vascular disease/ ischemia
- Post-irradiation
Obstruction- Oddi benign/ malignant stenosis
- Pancreas divisum
- Diverticula of duodenal window
- Duodenal polyps
- Vaterian ampulloma
- Periampullary duodenal cyst

Morphopathology

= process of fibrosis and sclerosis with pancreatic parenchymal destruction

Symptoms

  • Pain = major clinical symptom (upper abdomen, radiates into lumbar region; intensified by alcohol and fatty meals)
  • If 90% of acinar destroyed → insufficiency signs → steatorrhea
  • Malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins
  • Weight loss and muscular dysfunction
  • Diabetes (often requires insulin treatment)

DD

  • Pancreatic CA
  • Gallstones
  • AP
  • Gastric and duodenal ulcer
  • Gastric CA
  • IBS or IBD
  • Malabsorption syndromes

Complications

  • 1. Pain
  • 2. Pancreatic pseudocyst
  • 3. Bile duct stenosis
  • 4. Mesenteric/ splenic vein thrombosis
  • 5. Duodenal stenosis
  • 6. Pseudoaneurysm
  • 7. Pancreatic adenoCA
  • 8. Extrapancreatic malignant tumors

Treatment

  • Drug treatment → reducing pain, treatment of exocrine and endocrine pancreatic insufficiency
  • Special diet → excluding alcohol, tobacco, coffee, reduced fat and raw vegetables
  • Pain therapy → NSAID’s, tramadol
  • Insulin
  • Pancreatic replacement → lipase, trypsin (Kreon)
Surgery
Indications- Painful syndrome refractory to conservative treatment
- Suspicion of malignancy
- CBP obstruction
- Duodenal stenosis
- Pancreatic pseudocysts
- Intracystic bleeding, intraperitoneal or digestive bleeding
- Extrinsic compression of porto-mesenteric venous axis
Surgery for CP1. Drainage surgery
→ When Wirsung duct is dilated (> 7mm diameter) and consists in
pancreatico-jejunal anastomosis on Roux-en-Y limb of jejunum
2. Excision surgery → Pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure)
3. Denervation surgery → Bilateral thoracoscopic splanchnicectomy
Pseudocysts- US/ CT guided percutaneous drainage
- Endoscopic treatment → transpapillary drainage
- Surgery → drainage and excision
Jaundice- Stent or biliary-digestive bypass
Duodenal stenosisDuodenal stenosis- Gastro-entero anastomosis or pseudocyst drainage if this compresses the
stomach or duodenum

Benign tumors

= rare

Adenoma
Cystadenomaa) Serous (microcyst), no malignant potential
b) Mucinous cystadenomas, high malignancy potential, same therapeutic
strategy as in pancreatic CA
Cystic papillary tumor
Intraductal papillomaMay cause recurring acute pancreatitis and eventually obstructive chronic
pancreatitis

Clinical

  • Not characteristic
  • Abdominal pain or compression
  • May be palpable in epigastric region when large

Treatment

  • Surgery for symptomatic and/or voluminous tumors
  • Mucinous cystadenomas require organ and lymphatic resection

Malignant tumors

Epidemiology

  • 1% of all cancers, 10% of GI
  • Increasing incidence
  • Too rarely diagnosed on time to allow effective therapy

Risk factors

  • Age (60-80 y)
  • Smoking !!!
  • Alcohol
  • Diet - red meat and fats
  • Coffee
  • Familiy history due to association with other hereditary diseases (familial pancreatitis, Gardner’s snd, polycystic d.)
  • High risk disease (chronic pancreatitis, familial pancreatitis, Peutz-Jeghers, biliary lithiasis)
  • Genetic alterations → Oncogene (KRAS) or Tumor suppressor genes (CDKN2A, TP53, SMAD4)

Morphopathology

Macroscopic- Mostly located at pancreatic head (70%), then corpus (15%), tail (10%)
- Solid tumor, hard, irregular, yellowish grey
- In diffuse, multifocal forms, pancreas forms one single compact, hard tumoral mass
MicroscopicGX = Grade cannot be assessed
G1 = well differentiated tumor
G2 = moderately differentiated tumor
G3 = poorly differentiated tumor
G4 = undifferentiated tumor

Most important non-endocrine pancreatic CA types

  • 1. Severe ductal dysplasia/ carcinoma in situ
  • 2. Adenocarcinomas (ductal and acinar) → 81%
    • Squamous adenocarcinoma
    • Giant cell carcinoma
    • Cystadenomas
  • 3. Osteoclastic type tumors
  • 4. Serous cystadenocarcioma
  • 5. Mucinous cystadenocarcinoma
  • 6. Intraductal papillary mucinous carcinoma
  • 7. Acinar cell carcinoma
  • 8. Pancreatoblastoma
  • 9. Sarcomas
  • 10. Lymphomas

Pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasias (PanINs) – non-invasive proliferations of pancreatic ducts epithelium; classified by degree of nuclear atypias: PanIN-1, PanIN-2 → no oncological risk, PanIN-3 lesions → risk

Extension

  • Local invasion
  • Lymphatic
  • Hematogenic
  • Perineural (characteristic, loco-regional recurrences)
  • Pancreatic head carcinomas metastasize in liver, lungs and pleura
  • Corpus and tail in peritoneum

TNM classification

Tiscarcinoma in situ
T1tumor diameter ≤ 2cm, with no extension beyond pancreas
T2tumor limited to pancreatic gland, ≥ 2cm in diameter
T3extension of tumor beyond gland, but not invading superior mesenteric artery or celiac trunk
T4primary tumor invading celiac axis or superior mesenteric artery (unresectable)
N1regional lymph nodes with metastasis
M1remote metastases

Clinical

Status phase = clinical picture becomes suggestive for the locations → usually in advanced stage

Pancreatic headPancreatic bodyPancreatic tail
Triad: Jaundice, weight loss, pain
- Jaundice is usually first sign, but
shows advanced stage !
(80% unresectable)
- Earliest sign: dull, intermient pain in
epigastrium and left hypochondrium
- Advanced signs: Loss of appetite,
Nausea, Constipation or Diarrhea,
Fatigue, Fever
- Back pain → celiac plexus invasion
(final stage)
- DM → typically non-obese, no
family history, smoker, usually starts
few months before onset of jaundice
→ DM + progressive weight loss =
90% diagnostic specificity !
- Urine color = black beer
(choluric urine)
- Stool yellow, grey, white (acholic)
- Hepatomegaly
- Distended, tensed, hard, painless
gallbladder → Courvoisier Terrier’s
sign
- Repetitive attacks of acute
pancreatitis		- Rapid and very severe weight loss
- Later pain: very severe, more intense
during night, not influenced by eating,
radiating into back (Chauffard’s
pancratico-solar syndr.)
- Mental disturbances
- Anorexia, adynamia, vomiting
(duodenal stenosis due to invasion)
- Back pain - advanced, unresectable
case
- Migrant thrombophlebitis (Trousseau
sign) might occur months before
- Sectorial portal hypertension
syndrome with upper GI hemorrhage
due to ruptured esogastric varices
(splenic v. invasion)		- No specific clinical picture
- Continuous dull pain in LUQ,
constipation, DM, unspecific
dyspeptic syndrome, segmental
portal hypertension
- Hard palpable tumor, fixed,
transversal in epigastrium

General: left supraclavicular adenopathy (Virchow Troisier sign → distant metastasis), jaundiced, cachectic, ascites

Imaging

1. US- Cheap, non-invasive, largely accessible
- Tumors usually hypoechogenic with irregular contour
+ Enlarged spleno-portal axis, dilated CBD and intrahepatic bile ducts
+ Liver metastasis; lymph node involvement
+ Double duct sign (dilation of main bile and pancreatic ducts)
1.1 CEUS- Good for detecting liver metastasis (M)
1.2 Percutaneous US guided biopsy- Histological diagnosis
1.3 EUS- Almost 100% accuracy
- Only technique that detect tumors < 1cm (early cancers)
→ EUS-FNA – enough tissue samples ! (T)
- Negative biopsy does not exclude malignancy !
2. MDCECT= Multidetector contrast enhanced CT scan
- Using thin slices assessing local extension (T), detecting liver metastasis (M)
- Lymph nodes (N) > 1cm usually considered malignant
3. ERCP- Not currently used for diagnosis due to potential complications
4. TPC4. TPC= Transparietohepatic cholangiography
- Transparietal puncture under US/ CT guidance of dilated bile duct, contrast
into biliary tree
- Not currently used due to its complications (hemorrhage, bile leaks
(choleperitoneum), bile collection)
5. MRI- Higher specificity than CT scan
6. Angio-MRI- Detect tumoral invasion of adjacent vasculature → portal vein, SMA/V
7. Cholangio-MRI7. Cholangio-MRI- Most accurate technique in detecting bile intraductal obstacles (especially
small tumors)
- DD among periampullary tumors
8. Staging laparoscopy (SL)- Very useful in detecting “occult metastasis” (small, millimetric peritoneal
or hepatic deposits (undetectable even by most CTs)
- It is systematically indicated in ALL pancreatic body and tail CA’s
- Video-laparoscopy can be completed with laparoscopic ultrasonography,
for more accurate assessment of vascular peritumoral structures or small
intrahepatic mets

Treatment

Periampullary tumors !!! = tumors with different origin but same surgical treatment → ampullary tumors, distal cholangiocarcinoma, duodenal carcinoma, adenocarcinoma of pancreas head

  • I. Radical treatment
  • Only chance for cure R0
  • Pre-OP selection: T1, T2, T3, N0-M0, N1-M0 → only 15-25% are candidates
  • 5-year survival after is 10-25%
  • Pre-OP preparation
  • Jaundice
  • Malnutrition and malabsorbtion due to obstruction of bile ducts, pancreatic duct and/or duodenum
  • Hypoalbuinemia

Head ► Whipple (Cephalic Pancreatic-duodenoectomy)

  • Resection of
    • Gallbladder
    • Main bile duct
    • Gastric antrum + pylorum
    • Entire duodenum + 10-20cm from initial jejunum (first loop)
    • Pancreatic head
  • Digestive tract reconstruction
    • 1) pancreato-gastro or pancreato-jejunal
    • 2) hepatico-jejunal
    • 3) gastro-jejunal anastomoses
  • Weak pint: pancreatic stump and digestive tract → risk of fistula
  • Sometimes with subtotal/ total pancreatectomy to achieve R0

► Regional pancreatectomy

  • Including irresectable cases with posterior vascular invasion
  • After segmental resection of invaded vessels → restoration
  • portal vein - mesentero-portal end-to-end anastomosis (type I operation)
  • superior mesenteric artery - reimplantation into aorta (type II)
  • hepatic artery - interposing graft between it and aorta
  • Portal vein resection is justified (no morbidity/mortality), arterial resection not → contraindication !

(morbidity/mortality with no survival benefit)

► Pylorus preserving pancreatic duodenectomy/ Traverso-Longmire = gold standard
- Main advantage: significant earlier post-op weight gain and superior alimentary comfort due to
anatomical and functional integrity of stomach
- In severe jaundice → biliary decompression by stent/ external biliary drainage necessary before
radical OP to prevent fatal post-op acute liver failure
Body/ tail- Distal spleno-pancreatectomy
- Resectability and prognosis are even worse

Whipple

Distal spleno-pancreatectomy

Central pancreatectomy

  • II. Palliative treatment
  • 3 main therapeutical targets → jaundice, duodenal obstruction, pain
Jaundice- Biliary decompression via gall baldder, ductus choledocus or ductus hepaticus with
stomach, duodenum or jejunum
1. Choleocysto-duodenal or choleocysto-jejunal anastomosis
→ Nowadays exceptionally indicated in cases with very short life expectancy,
otherwise high chance of failure due to tumor invasion
2. Choledoco-duodenostomy
→ re-invasion likely
3. Roux-en Y hepatico-jejunostomy
- Main bile duct is transsected just below hilar bifurcation and anastomosed termino-
laterally to Roux en Y jejunal loop; eficient and has longest patency, invasion rarelly
occurs, bigger operation with bigger morbidity → only fit patients with longer (> 12-18
months) life expectancy (local extended, nonmetastatic)
Duodenal/ gastric outflow
obstruction		1. Gastroenterostomy
- Latero-lateral bypass, avoids duodenal stenosis
2. Double biliary and digestive diversion
- Only well selected cases → fit patients, locally advanced tumors, absence of any
detectable metastases (T3-4, N0-2, M0)
Pain- Chemical splanchnicectomy with alcohol = preferred nowadays
- Injection in celiac plexus
- Open, laparoscopic surgery, endosonography guiding, transgastric approach
- Also thoracoscopic splanchnicectomy possible

Radio- and chemotherapy

  • Radiotherapy - external or intraoperative radiation has no well documented results
  • Chemotherapy - at least 3 agents concomitantly, poor results
  • Chemotherapy + radiation therapy improves survival with advanced pancreatic cancer

I) Tumors of the endocrine pancreas

Insulinoma

  • Tumor of beta-islet cells → secretes insulin
  • Mostly benign insular adenoma, 10% malignant
  • Hypersecreting metastases may be cause of recurrence
  • Pathomorphology: small nodule, firm, located at head or tail of pancreas, can be ectopic
  • Neuropsychiatric manifestations
    • Central nervous: diplopia, convulsions, coma
    • Sympathetic nervous system: flushing, sweating, vomiting, persistent hunger
    • Psychiatric: restlessness, mental instability, disorientation
  • Signs and symptoms recurr at regular intervals → periodical bouts of hypoglycemia (after physical exercise or prolonged fasting) and subside postprandially (especially sweeets)
  • Clinical diagnosis based on Whipple triad
    • Insulin shock (hypoglycemia) induced by exercise or fasting
    • Low glycemia – under 50 mg% during bouts
    • Symptoms subside after glucose administration
  • Laboratory: glycemia, insulin, proinsulin, glucose/insulin ratio
  • Imaging: US (percutaneous, endoscopic, intraoperative), CT, MRI, angiography
  • Treatment: Radical surgical excision (local excision, central pancreatectomy, corporeo-caudal pancreatectomy, pancreaticoduodenectomy)
  • Radical resection evaluated intraoperativelly by measuring plasma insulin levels before and after excision !

Glucagonoma

  • Rare, mainly women
  • Pathomorphology: pancreatic body or tail (60%), extended to whole organ, head of gland (10%)
  • Often becomes malignant
  • Originates in glucagon secreting alpha cells
  • Clinical features: cutaneous lesions (migratory necrotising erythema), glossitis, vulvovaginitis, diabetes mellitus, anemia due to anorexia and hypoaminoacidemia, weight loss, antianabolic action, deep vein thrombosis
  • Treatment: surgical resection, tumor ablation even in presence of metastases, polychemotherapy
  • Repeated multiple re-excisions for local or metastatic recurrences prolong survival

Gastrinoma

  • Secreting gastrin → hypersecretion of HCl in stomach → gastric and duodenal ulcers (Zollinger-Ellison snd)
  • Eutopic (G cells in antrum, duodenal bulb, jejunum) or ectopic (pancreas, mesenteric ganglia, ovary, spleen)
  • Gastrinomas are often multiple (80%) and malignant (2/3 of cases)
  • Ulcers refractory to treatment, acid hypersecretion not influenced by treatment, diarrhea and steatorrhea due to large volume of gastric acid
  • Frequently with metastases at time of diagnosis
  • Treatment: suppression of acid secretion by high doses of H2 receptors blockers or omeprazol
  • Somatostatin analogs efficiently inhibit hormonal and gastric secretion (ocreotide)
  • Surgery - total gastrectomy (less common), vagotomy, tumor enucleation or corpo-caudal pancreatectomy

VIPoma

  • Originating in insular non-beta cells that secrete vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP)
  • Responsible for Verner-Morrison syndrome (watery diarrhea, hypokaliemia, hypochlorhydria, severe dehydration involving high fatal risk)
  • Pathomorphology - adenoma (43%), carcinoma (37%) or microadenomatosis
  • Clinical: diarrhea leading to severe dehydration with hypokaliemia, metabolic acidosis, hypomagnesemia (tetany), hypokalemic nephropathy with uremia, extreme physical fatigue, itchy rashes, heart disturbances (rhythm, failure)
  • Hypo-achlorhydria (strong inhibitor of acid gastric secretion)
  • Glucose intolerance
  • Treatment - surgical (corpo-caudal pancreatectomy), hydroelectrolithic rebalancing, administration of somatostatin analogs (Ocretotid, Sandostatin)

Somatostatinoma

  • Rare
  • High malignancy potential, with early metastases
  • Somatostatin triggers biliary lithiasis, diabetes mellitus, diarrhea and statorrhea
  • Inhibits somatotropic hormone, TSH, insulin, glucagons, gastrin, and cholecystokininpancreazimine scretions
  • Nausea, vomiting, bloating, weight loss
  • Treatment - surgical (cephalic duodeno-pancreatectomy or corpo-caudal pancreatectomy)

Pancreatic polypeptide secreting tumor

  • Clinical picture not specific, diarrhea, steatorrhea, basal hypochlorhydria, weight loss (inhibitory effect on gallbladder and pancreatic enzyme secretion)
  • Treatment - surgical (pancreaticoduodenectomy), streptozocin, somatostatin analogs

Carcinoid tumor

  • Rare, from chromaffin cells
  • Symptomatology not specific
  • Flushing, arterial hypertension, oedema around eyes, hypersecretion of saliva and tears, diarrhea, abdominal pain, all occurring in paroxistic bouts
  • High malignancy potential
  • Treatment - surgical (pancreaticoduodenectomy)

The pancreas Benign pancreatic disorders Acute pancreatitis

Ion Cosmin Puia

The 1992 International Symposium on Acute Pancreatitis defined acute pancreatitis as an acute inflammatory process of the pancreas with variable involvement of other regional tissues or remote organ systems. Acute pancreatitis can have mild and severe forms. In mild acute pancreatitis the organ dysfunction is minimal and the recovery without sequele. In severe acute pancreatitis (SAP) the pancreatic necrosis with complications and organ failure are always present.

The overall mortality is about 15%, but rises to 30% in severe AP and is much higher (50%) if the patient is older than 50 years. In SAP death in the first week is caused by organ failure. After the second week infection of the necrotic tissue can lead to septic shock.

The pancreas is a gland located in the uppermesocolic, retroperitoneal part of the abdomen .The insulin is produced by the ß –cells of the Langerhans islands. The exocrine secretion has an important role in the digestion of carbohydrates, fat, and protein. The enzymes are produced and then stored as inactive pro-enzymes in vesicles called zymogen. Through the Wirsung duct a variety of pancreatic enzymes get into the duodenum. The release of the proenzymes in the duct is triggered by the meal by several mechanisms:

  • vagal nerve
  • cholecystokinin (CCK)
  • secretin
  • vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP)
  • gastrin realeasing peptide (GRP) etc.

The first proenzyme to be activated by in the duodenum is trypsinogen. Trypsin continues the activation cascade of the other inactive enzymes.

There are several protective mechanisms against excessive or premature activation:

  • high levels of trypsin inhibit pancreatic secretion
  • separate packing of the proenzymes into the zymogen vesicles
  • combination of zymogen with protease inhibitors.

The abnormal activation cascade is started by an aggression which enables the lysosomes to activate the trypsinogen in the zymogen capsules. The intracellular activated enzymes get in the extracellular space. Their positive chemotactism for neutrophils and macrophages which release mediators aggravate the inflammation which eventually gets systemic. At Microlocal level the action on the vessels lead to edema, the elastase causing most circulation Damage of the damage to the vascular wall with subsequent hemorrhage and necrosis. The action of the inflammation mediators at general level can cause

& respiratory and renal complications leading to death. # = Severe Acute Pancreatitis (necrotizing Form) -Gallstones migrating into the common bile duct and irritating the sphincter of Oddi account for more than 1/3 of AP, being more frequent in women. Microstones and cholesterolosis are responsible of severe forms of AP because they can easily pass through the cystic duct and Oddi. It is not the blocking of the Oddi but the repetitive passage that irritates this highly reflexogenic area.

Alcohol is responsible of 1/3 of AP, affecting more men. Usually the ingestion of a large quantity of alcohol is combined with a fatty meal.

ERCP triggers in about 1-3% of the cases a AP, even in most experienced hands. Injecting iodinated contrast can raise the intraductal pressure enough to start the enzymatic cascade.

Hypertriglyceridemia can be the cause of severe forms of AP. It can be difficult to differentiate type I or V hyperlipidemia as a single cause of AP, as alcohol and fatty meals are also mentioned in the history of these cases.

Abdominal blunt trauma (bicycle, hoof, tire explosion) crush the pancreas against the spine. The lesion of other organs (duodenum) is usually associated. Penetrating injuries are easier to asses as the patient is usually operated for hemorrhage or peritonitis.

Drug-induced pancreatitis is usually mild. Drugs definitely associated with acute pancreatitis include azathioprine, sulfonamides, sulindac, tetracycline, valproic acid, didanosine, methyldopa, estrogens, furosemide, 6-mercaptopurine, pentamidine, 5-aminosalicylic acid compounds, corticosteroids, and octreotide.

The most common infectious cause of AP is mumps. Other viral induced AP are also mild forms, with a slight and transient elevation in amylase levels. Ascariasis as a cause for AP is encountered only in major infestations, when the worm is migrating through the Oddi in the common bile duct.

An obstructive primary or metastatic tumor can induce AP by increasing the intraductal pressure. The same mechanism can be blamed in abnormalities as pancreas divisum, which are associated with an impaired ductal drainage on the Santorini duct.

Postoperative or even iatrogenic AP is more frequent when the common bile duct is explored directly, with probes or during intraoperative cholagiography or manometry.

Hereditary pancreatitis is caused by the premature activation of trypsinogen. In mucoviscidosis AP is also more frequent.

Hypercalcemia, encoutered in hyperparathyroidism, toxic doses of vitamin D, and total parenteral nutrition is another cause of AP.

If no obvious cause can be identified the P can be labeled as idiopathic.

SYMPTOMS AND SIGNS

The abdominal pain has following characteristics:

  • severity
  • upper half of the abdomen
  • increasing intensity
  • posterior radiation
  • duration of several days (if not treated).

Fever has moderate values during the first days and is caused by inflamation not by infection. High fever is encountered after at least 2 weeks and is caused mostly by the infection of the necrotic areas.

Blood pressure is low and the heart rate high.

Bowel movements and passing of stool and gas are absent. Nausea and vomiting are almost defining AP.

The physical exam can mimic peptic ulcer peritonitis with intense pain, tenderness, guarding and rebound tenderness (Blumberg’s sign). Opposed to peritonitis the rectal exam is negative as the Douglas pouch is not irritated by any abdominal collection.When abdominal distension is most impressive occlusion can be the first diagnose. The bowel sounds are absent because of the reflex bowel paralysis. Early ascites can develop in severe forms. Lactescent ascites with a progressive accumulation can be encountered after 2-3 weeks of evolution.

The diffusion of the retroperitoneal hemorrhagic accumulation to the flanks (Grey Turner’s sign) is a late sign of AP. Because the umbilicus is almost free of properitoneal fatty tissue periumbilical ecchymoses can appear in hemorrhagic ascites (Cullen’s sign). Jaundice is more frequent in biliary AP but in severe cases it can be a sign of liver failure.

Dyspnea can be the result of subphrenic collections irritating the diaphragm, with or without a pleural effusion or, in severe AP, of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).

The circulating lipase may produce subcutaneous fat necrosis, clinically manifested by erythematous skin nodules.

The funduscopic examination can describe ischemic injuries in severe pancreatitis which can lead even to permanent blindness.

Uncoherence can be caused by the enzymatic aggression of phospholypase A on the sphingomielines of the nervous system.

DIFFERENTIALS

Every cause of acute abdomen must be considered in patients with AP. Some of them can be a cause of AP (cholelithiasis, choledocholithiasis) and others need emergency surgery:

  • Cholecystitis
  • Cholangitis
  • Duodenal or gastric perforated ulcer
  • Colonic Obstruction
  • Mesenteric infarction
  • Ectopic pregnancy.

Other causes of acute non-surgical abdomen or false acute abdomen must be ruled out, avoiding unnecessary surgical exploration, which in some cases can worsen the outcome:

  • Myocardial infarction
  • Bacterial pneumonia
  • Renouretheral colic.

LAB FINDINGS

Serum amylase and lipase levels must be 3 to 10 times higher than normal values ( depending on the units used) in order to label the case as AP.

Serum amylase or lipase values are of no help in differentiating a mild from a severe AP and do not have prognostic values.

Serum amylase are not specific for pancreatitis as higher values can be encountered in other diseases implying inflammation. The serum half-life of amylase is short so if the process subsides vales can return to normal after a few days. Urine amylase rises later but also return delayed to reference values. Normal serum amylase despite an obvious SAP indicates a total pancreatic necrosis, with no tissue left to produce the enzyme.

Lipase is more useful in confirming AP in delayed presentation as is has a longer half-life than amylase. It is also more specific but it is not routinely used in average hospitals.

Trypsin, trypsinogen, trypsinogen activation peptide can be measured but are not routinely used.

Cholestasis markers (alkaline phosphatase, total bilirubin) and citolysis enzymes (aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase) can indicate a gallstone triggered AP.

High cholesterol and triglycerides values can diagnose a type I or V hyperlipidemia as a cause of acute pancreatitis.

Hypocalcemia is secondary to the binding of calcium to the fatty acids resulting from the saponification (hydrolysis) of the fat. Rarely hypercalcemia can be the cause of AP.

Glucose can have high values in SAP but, as the endocrine functional reserves are important, it frequently returns within normal range.

The WBC is usually elevated, initially on behalf of inflammation and after at least one week because of the infection of necrotic tissue .

Hematocrit is usually high at admission because of edema and ascites. It may then drop in severe cases due to necrotic-hemorrhagic lesions.

C-reactive protein (CRP) higher 10 mg/dL at 48 hours after the onset of AP is a prognostic factor for organ failure. It must be stressed that CRP is not specific for P.

CRP is an acute-phase reactant that is not specific for pancreatitis.

Electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen, creatinin, arterial blood gases must be followed in order to diagnose any renal or respiratory problems.

IMAGING

Plain X-ray is not very useful any more but can describe:

  • pneumoperitoneum due to hollow organ perforation (differential )
  • paralitic ileus
  • the sentinel loop sign , described as the dilation of the first jejunal loop due to the proximity of P
  • the colon cut off sign, associates the dilation of the transverse colon with a empty of gas left flexure
  • calcifications in the pancreatic area ( stigmata of chronic pancreatitis). Abdominal ultrasound is of limited help because of the ileus. It

remains the technique of choice for detecting gallbladder lithiasis but it is

not reliable for common bile duct stones.

Abdominal CT scanning is the best imaging method in SAP, for an

accurate description of the affected areas. The Balthazar grading scale is

based on CT-findings.

  • A - Normal
  • B - Enlargement
  • C - Peripancreatic inflammation
  • D - Single fluid collection
  • E - Multiple fluid collections.

The risk of infection and mortality is none for A and B and rises from C to E.

CT (or, if possible ultrasound)-guided needle aspiration is important to asses the infection of the necrotic tissue. Usually there is a change in the pattern towards septic fever but the treatment can be better oriented if based on the antibiogram. The pus has to be examined immediately on a stain and cultures on for anaerobic bacteria and fungi are mandatory.

Dynamic spiral CT scanning offers superior data on the position and extent of pancreatic necrosis.

ERCP should be used with caution in biliary AP in the first 3 days from the onset. Later the lesions are already triggered and the risk of aggravating the process is high. Oddi shincter manometry is forbidden in AP.

Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography offers comparable information to ERCP without its risks.

Endoscopic ultrasound offers better data than plain ultrasound as the thickness of interposed tissue is diminished. The biopsy can be of help in differential diagnose.

In mild cases there is only edema of the retroperitoneal area, involving especially the peripancreatic tissue.

Severe AP is defined by necrosis of the retroperitoneal fat which can affect more remote areas like the mesentery or the Toldt fascia. In most of the cases the organs, including the pancreas are less affected than the surrounding fat. The fat suffers a cytosteatonecrosis which results in a typical aspect comparable with candle stains. The retroperitoneal edema and the ascites can have a hemorrhagic or biliary aspect.

PROGNOSIS

The Ranson score is the best known for trying to predict the evolution in AP. It can be calculated only the first 48 hours after the onset. The criteria for the first calculation are:

  • age > 55 years
  • WBC > 16000/ ml
  • serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) > 350 IU/l
  • ASAT > 250 IU/l
  • blood glucose > 200 mg/dl

The second, at 48 hours:

  • hematocrit decrease with > 10%
  • blood urea nitrogen increase more than 8 mg/dl
  • serum calcium < 8 mg/dl
  • arterial oxygen saturation < 60 mm Hg
  • base deficit > 4 mEq/l
  • estimated fluid sequestration > 6000 l. The mortality rises at 50% for a score over 5.

COMPLICATIONS

The pseudocyst is a collection of pancreatic fluid and necrotic debris enclosed by the neighboring organs having no walls of its own and lack an epithelial layer ( like true cysts). The granulative tissue that develops at its limits is mature after at least one month of evolution. Large or complicated pseudocysts need intervention.

The technique of choice is pseudocysto-jejunostomy, usually on an isolated Y loop. The isolated Y loop is better than the stomach or the duodenum because no food can get into the cavity and the better aspirative capacity of the jejunum. The risk of developing an abscess is thus avoided.

Transpapillary drainage can be useful in persistent external pancreatic fistulae or in communicating pseudocysts. A stent is left in place for a few weeks ensuring a proper drainage of the pancreatic secretion and relieving the pressure on the fistula or pseudocyst.

Percutaneous aspiration should be considered only as a mean to gain time in selected cases but not as a definitve treatment.

The transmural drainage of the pseudocysts raised hope in the '80 but, due to the small communication with the lumen of the stomach or duodenum, was more or less abandoned because of the high number of recurrences and abscesses.

Pancreatic abscesses and infected necrosis are complications that are caused by bacteria from the intestinal flora which migrate by translocation into the portal stream thus reaching the areas affected in the SAP. The percutaneaous drainage is seldom successful, even if more refined techniques like snares or basket-wires are used. The optimal moment of the open or laparoscopic removal of pus and necrotic tissue must be well chosen. The optimal timing is about 3-4 weeks after onset of the SAP, enough to allow a good delimitation of necrotic tissue, so the loss of blood and viable tissue is minimal. CT-guided needle aspiration is the only on able to ascertain infection but clinical criteria can also be used. If the favorable moment is lost the general status of the patient may worsen.

Pancreatic duct disruption is associated with extensive pancreatic necrosis. If drainage is in place the discharge has very high amylase values. If it communicates with a pseudocyst a volume augmentation will be observed. A transpapillary stent can be useful. If an external fistula persists for a time long enough to have a fibrotic tract a fistulo-jejunostomy on a Y loop should be performed. Pancreatic resections are seldom advisable.

Haemorrhage is fortunately rare. Due to the elastase the vessel wall may be affected at a various degree. Because it usually appears after a longer evolution adhesions make an open procedure difficult. If attempted, such an approach ends usually in a packing. Ultraselective angiography may localize the site and stop the bleeding by embolisation with various agents.

TREATMENT

On admission fluid resuscitation (crystalloids) has to be started without waiting for lab findings as edema and ascites sequestrate large fluid volumes. Starting with a bolus of 2-4 liters, 250-500 cc/h can be administered in order to ensure maintain hemodynamic stabilityand diuresis but taking care to avoid pulmonary edema.

In order to have an exact fluid balance a bladder catheter and a gastric aspiration are necessary.

Central venous lines and an arterial line are mandatory in patients with a poor status.

In order to minimize secretion and because of the ileus no oral intake is allowed.

Morphine has to be avoided because of the spastic effect on Oddi, but a correct analgesia is mandatory.

Oral intake has to be started as soon as gastric plegia resumes.

There is a corelation between the pancreatic necrosis, bacterial contamination and sistemic complications. The mortality rises if the infection is present .

Some studies do not recommend antibioprofilaxy in al patients with necrotic AP, but only in some high risk groups and if complications occur.

The choice of AB between meropenem vs imipenem (standard of treatment in necrotic AP) does not demonstrate any advantage for one of them.

The treatment duration for imipenem is at least 14 days, or more if systemic complications occur. A longer period of time reduces the mortality but not the septic complications. The treatment can start after 96 from the onset of SAP. An early start seems to lower mortality.

The selection of antibioticoresistant germs in patients with a longer stay on ICU and longer treatment could be demonstrated in about 50% cases of SAP.

Antifungal prophylaxis can be obtained with fluconazol or garlicin but , in a fungal systemic infection, fluconazol is ineffective and amphotericin B has to be used (He)

The use of octreotide (somatostatin) in the first days may improve the outcome inSAP.

After an initial enthusiasm the use of protease inhibitors (Gordox) was abandoned.

Hemodiafiltration (CHDF) on polimetilmetacrilat (PMMA) membranes helps in eliminating cytokines.

Selective digestive decontamination (SDD) is also recommended. It consists in unabsorbable AB and it is recommended only for selected patients.

The continuous regional arterial infusion (CRAI) with protease inhibitors and AB reduces ischemia and the hipoperfusion due to the vasospasm in the initial stage of the disease.

Combining SDD, early enteral nutrition (EN) and CRAI mortality dropped from 23 to 6%.

Total parenteral nutrition is not routinely recommended. An endoscopically assisted nasojejunal feeding tube or a surgical jejunostomy is preferred. Keeping the bowel active helps maintaining a balanced intestinal flora. Lactobacillus plantarum 299 as a probiotic and oat fibers as a prebiotic have a similar effect.

Surgery has certain guidelines recommended by Werner and Buchler in 2003:

  • it has to be avoided the first two weeks (Isaji recommends surgery at 4 weeks after the onset).
  • sterile necrosis has to be treated in a conservative manner
  • sterile necrosis can benefit from surgery if there is a tendency to extension or in fulminant AP ( defined by organ failure at less than 72 from onset)
  • the infection of necrotic pancreatic or peripancreatic tissue has to be operated
  • the technique must evacuate the necrosis but has to spare as much tissue as possible
  • colecystectomy is mandatory in every gallstone P or even idiopathic AP to avoid recurrence.
  • minimally invasive approach has to be limited to highly specialized centers.

The classic approach is planned staged re-laparotomies for necrosectomy with abundant lavage. The disadvantage is that each time general anesthesia is necessary, frequently in a frail patient.

Necrosectomy can be combined with closed continuous lavage ( lower morbidity) or with laparostomy ( in extensive necrosis). The closed lavage consists in placing several drains in and around the omental pouch and irrigating on some tubes with several liters a day of saline solution while on others tle liquid is evacuated. The idea is that the flow will wash away the necrotic debris but after 48 hours the circuit is practically blocked by adhesions so it becomes inefficient.

The laparostomy allows an easier access to the omental pouch so necrosectomy can be done as frequently as needed. It consists in suturing the opened gastrocolic ligament to the parietal peritoneum and aponevrosis. It has a higher morbidity (fistulae, bleeding etc.) and is certainly followed by an incisional hernia. A special zipper offers the advantages of laparostomy while partially avoiding the drawbacks.

A special kind of laparostomy is the Vac-pac indicated in SAP with abdominal hypertension and compartment syndrome. A protective layer is put over the viscera and a second layer covers the incision. Between them an aspiration tube keeps the edges of the laparostomy together. Delayed aponevrotic suture after at least 5 days ensures per primam healing.

In 1996 Gagner described laparoscopic debridement and necrosectomy in SAP. Access is possible by all the classical abdominal ways but also by retroperitoneoscopy. Because of the method limits conversion must be kept at a low threshold, otherwise serious complications may be encountered.

Chronic pancreatitis

Florin Graur, Ion Catirau

DEFINITION

Chronic pancreatitis is a continuing inflammatory pathology of the pancreas leading to irreversible morphologic changes, which causes exocrine and endocrine pancreatic insufficiency.

EPIDEMIOLOGY

The lack of a simple and universally accepted definition of chronic pancreatitis determine the variability of statistics. Such chronic pancreatitis incidence vary widely from country to country. In Switzerland chronic pancreatitis incidence is 1.6 / 100,000 new cases per year. In the United States the incidence and prevalence of chronic pancreatitis is 4 / 100,000 and 13 / 100,000, respectively. In Romania, the disease has a prevalence of 5.19 / 100,000 of inhabitants.

ETIOLOGY

The main cause of chronic pancreatitis (up to 70%) is alcoholism. Recent studies have demonstrated that the etiology of chronic pancreatitis is complex and often multifactorial, which is why it was proposed TIGAR-O classification system of the etiology of chronic pancreatitis (Table 1).

It is worth mentioning that only 5-10% of drinkers develop chronic pancreatitis, which demonstrates the multifactorial nature of pathology. With improved diagnostic methods the number of cases of idiopathic chronic pancreatitis are greatly reduced. Hereditary chronic pancreatitis has early onset, before the age of 20 years. Chronic autoimmune pancreatitis develops in other autoimmune diseases (Sjogren syndrome, primary biliary cirrhosis) and require immunosuppressive therapy. Chronic pancreatitis can occur in patients with endocrine disorders, it may be present in hyperparathyroidism and is a rare form. Increased levels of serum calcium levels determine its submission to the pancreatic parenchyma with pancreatic canaliculi obstruction

PATHOGENESIS:

At present there is no unanimity regarding the pathogenesis of chronic pancreatitis. There are many theories, but none pathogenic theory not explain the entire chain.

The main theories developed to date are:

  • Oxidative stress theory: bile reflux of oxygen free radicals synthesized

in the liver

  • Theory of ductal obstruction: Alcohol produce sedimentation of

proteins from pancreatic juice in pancreatic ducts

  • Autoimmune theory
  • Theory of pancreatic necrosis - fibrosis: chronic pancreatitis occurs due

to repeated episodes of acute pancreatitis.

MORPHOPATHOLOGY:

Morphological appearance of chronic pancreatitis consists of a process of fibrosis and sclerosis with pancreatic parenchymal destruction. Macroscopic appearance is characterized by a firm consistency of the pancreas, which can be increased in volume or atrophic

Cremer classified on grounds of severity chronic pancreatitis in six stages:

  • Stage 1: minimal damage detected in small pancreatic ducts;
  • Stage 2: Wirsung duct slightly irregular;
  • Stage 3: cystic dilatation of one or more focal lobular canaliculi;
  • Stage 4: stone (single or multiple) in the duct of Wirsung without

upstream dilation;

  • Stage 5: cephalic pancreatitis with a long stenosis of Wirsung duct at

this level;

  • Stage 6: pancreatitis with complete stenosis of Wirsung duct in cephalic

pancreas;

SYMPTOMS:

Pain is the major clinical symptom in chronic pancreatitis and is associated with exocrine and endocrine pancreatic insufficiency symptoms. Abdominal pain is localized in the upper abdomen and radiate in lumbar region, is intense, it can be persistent or recurrent. The pain is intensified by alcohol and fatty foods. If the disease is advanced, the exocrine function is largely lost, on much of the patients the pain diminishes. Pain relief can be obtained by position adopted by patients with knee flexed to the abdomen. The pain is so intense that it may require administration of analgesics (opioids).

If 90% of acinar pancreatic structure is destroyed, pancreatic exocrine insufficiency signs occurs. Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency is caused by low levels or absence of pancreatic enzymes, which lead to steatorrhea. Steatorrhea is appearance of abundant and acholic stools. Malabsorption of fat soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) is associated. Malabsorption secondary to exocrine pancreatic insufficiency cause weight loss and muscle dysfunction.

Endocrine failure is not installed with the exocrine and usually appears late. Diabetes in chronic pancreatitis rarely respond to treatment with oral antidiabetic agents and requiring insulin therapy, but in these patients glucagon levels are altered, so are at risk of developing severe hypoglycemia, therefore requires strict surveillance of insulin therapy.

LABORATORY EXAMINATIONS

The diagnosis of chronic pancreatitis is difficult in its early stages, a whole diagnostic explorations include laboratory tests, functional tests, imaging and endoscopic explorations.

Laboratory tests include the determination of:

  • serum amylase and lipase: normal or slightly elevated
  • ionogram: hypo-Na and hypo-K
  • glycaemia: elevated in endocrine failure
  • bilirubin, transaminases: increased during compression of main bile

duct

  • total proteins: decreased due to malabsorption

Exocrine pancreatic function tests

Test by exogenous stimulation with secretin-cholecystokinin - measured secretion of bicarbonate, trypsin and amylase (sensitivity of 75%)

Evaluation of pancreatic endocrine function is made by glucose tolerance test, and glycosuria determination and glucose level in blood

Abdominal radiography with no preparation - may identify calcification in 30% cases in the pancreatic lodge or pancreatic duct stones.

IMAGING EXAMS

Abdominal ultrasound - is the first investigation that should be considered when chronic pancreatitis is suspected. May show hypertrophy or atrophy of the gland, calcifications and possible complications (pseudocyst), can perform biopsy by ultrasound guidance, useful in pseudotumor form of chronic pancreatitis

Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) - is both a diagnostic and therapeutic method. It highlights dilatation or stenosis of the Wirsung, ductal communication of pancreatic pseudocysts, bile duct stenosis.

Endoscopic ultrasonography - the advantages of this imaging method is its non-invasive character, ability to obtain biopsies by puncture with fine needle aspiration (FNA) useful in the differential diagnosis of pseudotumoral pancreatitis with pancreatic cancer

Abdominal CT contrast enhanced - highlights the volume changes of the pancreas, Wirsung dilatation, pancreatic pseudocysts presence, changes in caliber of the common bile duct

MRI - administration of secretin increases the sensitivity of the examination. Colangio - MRI provides the ability to visualize pancreatic and biliary ductal system by a non-invasive method without ionizing radiation.

DIFFERENTIALS:

The differential diagnosis in chronic pancreatitis will do primarily with a malignant pancreatic tumor. Pancreatic carcinoma can simulate the symptoms of chronic pancreatitis or chronic pancreatitis can be a risk factor for the development of carcinoma. If there is an extreme situation, radical surgery is required because it is the treatment of neoplasia, and in case of chronic pancreatitis ensure adequate pancreatic drainage. Other conditions require differential diagnosis are: gallstones, acute pancreatitis, gastric and duodenal ulcers, gastric cancer, irritable bowel syndrome, malabsorption syndromes, Crohn's disease.

COMPLICATIONS:

COMPLICATIONS OF CHRONIC PANCREATITIS:

Pain 90%

Pancreatic pseudocysts 25% -30%

Bile duct stenosis 10% -15%

Mesenteric venous thrombosis 5% -10%

Duodenal stenosis 4% -5%

Pseudoaneurysm 2% -3%

Pancreatic adenocarcinoma 2% -4%

Extrapancreatic malign tumors 10-15%

Pancreatic pseudocyst by definition is an extra- or intra-pancreatic collection of pancreatic fluid, without a proper wall, not coated with epithelium and may contain pancreatic juice, necrosis, blood or pus.

These occur due to the rupture of pancreatic ductal system secondary to lumenal overpressure. Pseudocysts may be asymptomatic or manifested by pain, clinical signs related to compression of neighboring organs (CBP, stomach, duodenum) or their complications (bleeding, infection, rupture), in most cases require surgical treatment - drainage procedures.

Main bile duct stenosis in its terminal portion is secondary to pancreatic fibrosis.

Splenic vein thrombosis cause sectorial portal hypertension, which is manifested as upper gastrointestinal bleeding from gastric varices. Most surgeons reserve splenectomy in the treatment of splenic vein thrombosis in episodes with massive upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage.

Arterial pseudoaneurysms commonly occur in patients with pancreatic pseudocyst.

Lowenfels et al. demonstrated that the incidence of pancreatic cancer after 10 years of chronic pancreatitis is 1.8% and 4% after 20 years. Chronic inflammatory changes in the pancreatic parenchyma make the diagnosis of pancreatic cancer difficult.

Treatment of chronic pancreatitis

Drug treatment has three main objectives: reducing pain, treatment of exocrine and endocrine pancreatic insufficiency.

Patients with chronic pancreatitis require a special diet, excluding alcohol, tobacco, coffee, and reduce the amount of ingested fat and raw vegetables.

Pain therapy begins by administration of NSAID. If the pain does not decrease, a centrally acting analgesic (Tramadol) should be associated, and if such association fails to relieve pain, opioid analgesics should be administered.

The treatment of exocrine pancreatic insufficiency is substitutive and consists of the administration of pancreatic enzymes (lipase, trypsin).

Insulin is necessary in patients with endocrine pancreatic insufficiency and in such patients slightly higher than normal blood glucose values should be maintained because the process of fibrosis involved and pancreatic alpha cells that produce glucagon.

SURGERY

Indications for surgery:

  • painful syndrome refractory to conservative treatment
  • suspicion of malignancy
  • CBP obstruction
  • duodenal stenosis
  • pancreatic pseudocysts
  • intracystic bleeding, intraperitoneal or digestive bleeding
  • extrinsic compression of porto-mesenteric venous axis

Surgery for chronic pancreatitis are classified into three categories:

1. drainage surgery

2. excision surgery

3. denervation surgery

-Drainage surgery:

This treatment should be applied when Wirsung duct is dilated (> 7mm diameter) and consists in pancreatico-jejunal anastomosis on Roux-en-Y limb of jejunum. Puestow and Gillesby propose in 1958 pancreatico – jejunoanastomosis side-to-side on Roux-en-Y limb of jejunum. The surgery consists of an incision of the pancreatic duct to the left of mesenteric vessels and ascends a Roux-en-Y loop through a breach in transvers mesocolon and performing longitudinal pancreatico-jejunoanastomosis L-L. Partington and Rochelle change technique exposed above by cutting pancreatic duct from the pancreatic head and continue to the tail of the pancreas, followed by side-to-side longitudinal pancreatico-jejunoanastomosis on Roux-en-Y limb of jejunum.

  • Excision surgery:

Pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure)

Surgery consists of block excision that includes gastric antrum, duodenum, pancreatic head, first jejunal loop, bile duct and gallbladder. Restores digestive continuity by making pancreatico-jejunoanastomosis, hepatico-jejunoanastomosis and gastro-enteroanastomosis. This surgery removes the zone of inflammatory changes in the pancreatic head and preserves the body and tail of the pancreas, exocrine and endocrine pancreatic function, respectively.

Pancreaticoduodenectomy can be performed with preservation of the pylorus (Traverso-Longmire procedure).

Duodenum-Preserving Resection of the Pancreatic Head (Beger procedure)

It consists of a subtotal resection of the pancreatic head, keeping a rim of pancreatic tissue tangential to the duodenum, to protect the vasculature. Duodenum with stomach, main bile duct, body and tail of the pancreas are not excised. This surgical procedure removes the inflammatory process of the pancreatic head, ensure decompression/drainage of Wirsung, main bile duct and preserve exocrine and endocrine functions of the pancreas. After pancreatic resection, an end-to-side or side-to-side pancreaticojejunoanastomosis on Roux-en-Y limb of jejunum will be performed and an side-to-side anastomosis between the rim of pancreatic tissue tangential to the duodenum and ascended jejunal loop.

Local resection of the pancreatic head with lateral pancreaticojejunostomy (Frey procedure).

This surgery consists in pancreatic head resection with longitudinal lateral pancreatico-jejuno-anastomosis without posterior tunneling of pancreas and without cutting the pancreas anterior to the superior mesenteric vessels. The purpose of this surgery is to drain the Wirsung duct and secondary pancreatic ducts, excision of cephalic pancreatic parenchyma with nerve structures and opening the Wirsung duct at the level of pancreatic body ant tail which will be anastomosed with a Roux-en-Y jejunal loop.

Another excision procedure is the Berne procedure, proposed by Buechler et al, it is a modified version of Beger procedure and consist in pancreatic head excision with restoring digestive continuity through an pancreatico-jejunoanastomosis on Roux-en-Y limb of jejunum. This procedure avoids dissection of the pancreas from the portal vein

-Distal pancreatectomy

It is indicated in patients with pathology limited to the body or tail of the pancreas and Wirsung duct diameter <5mm and may or may not be associated with splenectomy. Surgery consists of resection of the pancreas tail and part of the body followed by pancreatic stump suture or end-to-side pancreaticojejunal anastomosis.

  • Total pancreatectomy

It is indicated in patients with persistent pain, which partial resection had no effect and those with total exocrine and endocrine insufficiency.

  • Denervation surgery

Bilateral thoracoscopic splanchnicectomy

Consist in splanchnic nerve resection and its branches through thoracoscopic approach

Treatment of chronic pancreatitis complications:

Pseudocysts

  • Ultrasound or CT guided percutaneous drainage
  • Endoscopic treatment: transpapillary drainage when pseudocyst

communicate with the main pancreatic duct or transmural drainage between pseudocyst and a digestive organ close to pseudocyst (stomach, duodenum).

  • Surgery: involves two types of surgery, drainage and excision. The

drainage procedure involves an anastomosis between pseudocyst and a segment from the digestive tract, which is chosen depending on the location of the pseudocyst (stomach, duodenum, jejunum).

Jaundice

It can be solved by fitting a endoscopic prosthesis at the site of stenosis of main bile duct or by surgery doing a biliary-digestive by-pass.

Duodenal stenosis

Can be solved by gastro-enteroanastomosis or pseudocyst drainage if this compresses the stomach or duodenum.

Tumors of the pancreas

Doru Munteanu

There are tumors of the exocrine pancreas and tumors of the endocrine pancreas, benign and malignant.

TUMORS OF THE EXOCRINE PANCREAS

BENIGN TUMORS

These types of tumors are rare. Due to the scarcity of the clinical picture, they are detected accidentally on the occasion of an imagistic (ultrasound or CT-scan) checkup or a laparotomy for another disorder, sometimes even at necropsy. Histopathologically, they are: adenomas, cysts, cystadenomas, solid cystic tumors and intraductal papillomas.

a) Adenoma. Depending on the tissue of origin they may be ductal, acinar or mixed. They present in the form of solid tumors, unique or multiple, sometimes encapsulated. Well vascularized, they may be detected clinically under the form of pulsatile tumoral masses, and paraclinically by angiography.

Cysts may be small or very large, unique or multiple, mostly benign.

b) Cystadenoma has two variants: serous (microcyst), presenting calcifications and developing from acinar cells. Mainly found at the pancreatic tail or head, they do not become malignant. Mucinous cystadenomas though, have a high malignancy potential (borderline tumors); such cases require same therapeutic strategyas in pancreatic cancer.

c) Cystic papillary tumors, occur more frequent in young women, are located at the tail or head of the pancreas. They present cystic areas alternating with solid ones, are very rare and reach considerable dimensions; well encapsulated, they can be easily cleaved from the surrounding normal pancreatic tissue.

d) Intraductal papilloma may become obstructive, responsible for multiple bouts of recurring acute pancreatitis and eventually obstructive chronic pancreatitis.

DIAGNOSIS

The clinical features are not characteristic, lacking in specific elements. Abdominal pain or compression on the adjacent organs may appear. The tumor may be palpated in the epigastric region when large.

Paraclinical examinations: ultrasound, a non-invasive technique, is very useful as it locates the tumor. Histological samples may be obtained by USguided puncture biopsy. CT scans, MRI, angiography and retrograde endoscopic pancreatography are also used, but the highest diagnostic accuracy is reached by the endoscopic ultrasound examination which also offers the possibility of biopsy under direct US visual control.

TREATMENT- is surgical for symptomatic and/or voluminous tumors and consists of ablation. Mucinous cystadenomas require organ and lymphatic resection, not just tumor removal, due to their high malignant potential.

MALIGNANT TUMORS

They represent about 1% of all neoplasms and 10% of digestive cancers.

Pancreatic adneocarcinoma continues to be a gloomy issue of digestive pathology, with increasing incidence. It still is too rarely diagnosed on time to allow for an effective therapy. For 60 to 80% of the patients with pancreatic head carcinoma, jaundice is the “initial” clinical sign, meaning, the one that brings the patient to the clinician (although, in fact, not an early clinical sign at all!). From these, 20% at the most may be submitted to surgery, and only 10% of the resectad ones will be eventually truly cured. The result is quite disappointing as finally, only 1% of all the patients with pancreatic cancer are radically cured ( more optimistic statistics do also exist).

EPIDEMIOLOGY

  • Morbidity of pancreatic cancers increases from east to west, reaching a

maximum in western European developed countries and North America (12/100,000 population).

-.Mortality rate is highest in the USA (fourth cause of death) and western, developed countries (10-12/100,000 population and about 5/100,000 in Italy and Japan); In Romania mortality is 5.2 for men and 2.7 for women (in 100,000 population).

Risk factors:

-Age: most cases occure between 60 and 80 years of age, mainly in men. Familial incidence, though rare, suggests the involvement ofgenetic factors (the association ofpancreatic cancer with hereditary diseases is an important genetic marker, for example familial pancreatitis, Gardner’s syndrome, polycystic disease).

-Smoking is proved as the most important and clearly defined pancreatic cancer risk factor; carcinogenic tobacco metabolites (nitrosamines) excreted by the bile, reach the pancreatic ducts, causing hyperplasic injuries. Cancer risk in smokers is about three times higher than in non-smokers (25-30% of cases are caused by smoking!).

-Alcohol, though known to be aggressive on the pancreas, has not been yet documented in the etiology of cancer.

-Diet is incriminated in pancreatic carcinogenesis. Excess ofred meat and especially fats (biliary secretion of cholecystokinine), by stimulation of hypersecreting pancreatic cells proliferation predisposes to cancer, while vegetables and fruit have a protective effect.

-Coffee is also positively correlated with increased morbidity of pancreatic cancer.

-High risk diseases: calcifying chronic pancreatitis, familial pancreatitis, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.Association with biliary disorders was more frequently reported in women (biliary lithiasis), being attributed to the bilioduodenal reflux, rich in carcinogenic substances, into the pancreatic ducts.

-Genetic alterations:-- oncogenes generate an increased state of activation, thus multiplying the risk of malignant proliferation. KRAS, with a mutation rate of over 90%, is the most frequently mutated oncogene in ductal adenocarcinoma of the pancreas;

-- Tumor-suppressor genes when active, have a protective effect against tumoral proliferation; in pancreatic cancer, some of these genes are inactivated. The most frequently mutated tumor-suppressor genes are CDKN2A, TP53, and SMAD4, mutated in 85%, 75%, and 55% of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma cases respective

PATHOMORPHOLOGY:

Macroscopical findings: pancreatic malignant tumors are mostly located at the pancreatic head (70%), then corpus (15%), and tail (10%). More than one tumoral focimay be found rarely aswel (5-10%). It presents as a solid tumor, hard, irregular, yellowish grey. In diffuse, multifocal forms, the pancreas forms one single compact, hard tumoral mass.

Histologically there are well differentiated forms, with a slower evolution, and non-differentiated ones, extremely aggressive. From this point of view, the following grading system is currently used:

GX = Grade cannot be assessed

G2 = moderately differentiated tumor

G3 = poorly differentiated tumor

G4 = undifferentiated tumor.

Histopathologically -the most important nonendocrine pancreatic carcinoma types are:

-Severe ductal dysplasia/carcinoma in situ (PanInIII; pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia)

-Adenocarcinomas (ducatal and acinar)

-adenosquamous carcinoma

-giant cell carcinoma

-cystadenomas

-Osteoclastic type tumors

-Serous cystadenocarcioma

-Mucinous cystadenocarcinoma

-Intraductal papillary mucinous carcinoma

-Acinar cell carcinoma

-Pancreatoblastoma

-Sarcomas

-Lymphomas.

By far the most frequent histological variety of nonendocrine malignant tumors of the pancreas is the ductal adenocarcinoma (81%).

The tumor extends by local invasion, but lymphatic, hematogenic and perineural dissemination are common aswell; (perineural dissemination is actually characteristic for pancreatic adenocarcinomas and explaines some late loco-regional recurrences after apparently radical resections). Generally, pancreatic head carcinomas metastasize in the liver, lungs and pleura, while the ones in the corpus and tail, in the peritoneum as well.

-Pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasias (PanINs) are noninvasive proliferations of the pancreatic ducts’ epithelium; they are classified by the degree of nuclear atypias as follows: PanIN-1, PanIN-2, with minimal and moderate atypias respectively; these two types do not present oncological risk. On the other hand, PanIN-3 lesions (severe epithelial atypias), present a significant risk, as they can give rise to infiltrating ductal adenocarcinoma of the pancreas. This is the reason why, PanIN-3 lesions have been recently included in the ( last edition of the American Joint Commettee on Cancer, Cancer Staging Manual), histopathological classification of pancreatic cancer.
