CLINICAL FEATURES

From this point of view, a clinical distinction must be made between the pancreatic head tumors and the ones located at the body or tale of the gland.

Pancreatic head carcinoma (PHC): the most common is the symptomatic triad: jaundice,body weight loss, pain.

Two periods have been described from the point of view of the clinical manifestations: onset (till diagnosis) and status. Other clinicians make use of other two periods: prior to and after onset of jaundice. However, these scholastic divisions and periods were not of much help, nor was the classic opinion of some that jaundice, in PHC, is an early clinical sign. On the contrary, although jaundice, once occurred, makes the patient apply for the initial medical consultation in most of the cases, in this phase the diagnosis comes too late for a treatment with curative intent (in more than 80% of the cases). Thus jaundice is in fact a late and not an early clinical sign !

In this case, if jaundice is not a real early sign is there one ?

Onsetis insidious with various symptoms, not organ specific. The most common complain is dull and intermient pain in the epigastrium and left hypochondrium; afteryears it’s intensity grows progressively radiating to the back and lumbar area, then exacerbated when lying down, subsiding when thighs are flexed to the abdomen or by standing, followed by weight loss,loss of appetite, nausea, jaundice,physical fatigue, fever, constipation or diarrhea, in advanced stages.

In late, finalstages of the disease, due to the tumor’s inavasion of the celiac plexuses, the intensity of pain becomes exruciating, unbearable,necessitating opioids or spalnchnicectomy; it is the so called “back pain”which signifies, without any imagistic, that the case is unresectable, sometimes not even surgical anymore.

Diabetes mellitus deserves here a special mention, as it seems to be, in some cases, a real early metabolic disturbance, which, when identified in due time and correctly interpreted, might lead to an early diagnosis of a pancreatic cancer, as it might occur 18 to 24 months prior to jaundice ! This special type of diabetes: occures usually in nonobese male patients in their 60’s, smokers, with no familial history of diabetes. THIS PATERN SHOULD DRAW YOUR ATENTION !When asociated with progressive weight loss it might have a diagnostic specificity of 90%!

Recurrent, repetitive attacks of acute pancreatitis (drinking, biliary or metabolic etiology excuded) can be, in 1.4-3% of cases, generated by a pancreatic main ducttumoral obstruction.

This phase lasts on an average 18-24 months before jaundice occures !

In thestatus phase the clinical picture becomes suggestive for the locations to the head, corpus or tail (yet, I’ll have to repeat, this phase is for most of the cases a late one).

  • In pancreatic head located tumors, the clinical picture is dominated by

jaundice, with the typical features for a malignant biliary obstruction: (jaundice with slow progressive onset, painless, no fever, no remissions, possibly even turning into “black jaundice”). Refractory, unbearable, pruritus is associated. Moreover, pruritus might even precede jaundice with several weeks ! Urine is colored-aspect similar with black beer- (choluric urine), stools become yellow or grey, even white ( a-cholic stools), hepatomegaly appears. In 33% of the cases a distended, tensed, hard, painless gallbladder can be typiacally seen and palpated in the right upper abdominal quadrant (Courvoisier-Terrier’s sign). All the other symptoms and signs aggravate, especially weight loss which finally becomes impressive (cachexia).

Remember, when diagnosed in a jaundiced patient, pancreatic head carcinoma is in 80% of the cases unresectable !

  • In pancreatic boady carcinoma (PBC) two elements are characteristic:

1. - rapid and severe weight loss (the most intense body weight loss described in human semiology), the patient “shrinking down” each day, sometimes in spite of a normal appetite, painless;

2. - later, pain occurs; very intense, constant or in bouts, more severe during nights, not influenced by feeding, radiating to the back (Chauffard’s pancratico-solarsyndrome), due to the invasion of the solar plexus, occures in the advanced phases of the disease.

3. - Mental disturbances may appear.

4. - Anorexia, adynamia, vomiting (duodenal stenosis due to direct invasion).

5. - The specific type of pain, the “back pain,” defines an advanced, unresectable case, beyond any imaging.

6. - Migrant thrombophlebitis (Trousseau sign) is typically associated with pancreatic body cancers ( head locations as well); it might occur months before diagnosis.

7. - Sectorial portal hypertension syndrome with upper digestive tract hemorrhage due to ruptured esogastric varices, might be the initial clinical manifestation for this location (splenic vein abutment/invasion). Rarely, sudden, fulminant upper digestive tract hemorrhages, generated by direct tumoral invasion/erosion of the splenic artery through the posterior gastric wall, may occur as well.

  • In pancreatic tail carcinomas (PTC) there isn’t a specific clinical

picture. Continuous dull pain in the left upper abdominal quadrant may be accompanied by constipation, diabetes mellitus, unspecific dyspeptic syndrome, signs of segmental portal hypertension.

In very advanced stages, in a jaundiced and cachectic patient with recent diabetes mellitus and no family history, digestive phenomena reflecting the invasion or the compression ofadjacent organs (stomach, duodenum, colon), a hard palpable tumor, fixed, transversal in the epigastrium, frequently associated with ascites (more common in the corpus or tail locations), possibly left supraclavicular adenopathy (Virchow-Troisier sign).

IMAGING

When evaluating a cancer case, positive diagnosis (confirmation of location with histologic proof), is followed by an as accurate as possible staging process, during which the T, N and M categories are evaluated ( T – local extension of tumor, N – lymph node status and M -presence/absence of distant metastases) which finally will make it possible to select the most efficient therapeutic protocol for the individual case.

1.Ultrasonography is a helpful examination in pancreatic cancer; it is cheap, noninvasive, largely accessible. It frequently is the initial imagistic technique used.Volume changes of the gland generate the “tumoral syndrome”.

Pancreatic malignant tumors usually are hypo-echogenic as compared to normal pancreas, with irregular contour.

Changes in the adjacent anatomical structures (enlarged spleno-portal axis, dilated CBD and intrahepatic bile ducts, distended gallbladder, dilated main pancreatic duct). Liver metastases and/or lymph nodes involvement are also assessed.

The “double duct sign”, consists of concomitant dilation of both main bile and pancreatic ducts; it is an indirect imagistic sign of a distal periampullar obstacle, even in cases in which the tumor has not yet been detected.Gallbladder and intrahepatic bile ducts are dilated as well.

Sensibility/specificity is 65-75%. Tumors smaller than 1.5-2cm might be missed.

  • Contrast enhanced ultrasonography (CEUS) reaches high levels of

accuracy in detecting liver mets (M cathegory).

  • Percutaneous US-guided biopsy is a technique providing high accuracy

and makes possible a histological diagnosis in 93% of the cases. Puncture guided by CT, or US may reach 100% accuracy, without negative results.

  • - Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) examination, a technique developed in

the last 30 years, provides diagnostic accuracy in almost 100% of the cases; it is the only technique able to detect tumors smaller than 1 cm (early pancreatic cancers !); concomitant EUS-FNA guided biopsy can confirm the diagnosis; anyway, a negative biopsy does not exclude malignancy !!; in these cases, when malignancy is strongly suspected, several passages with the biopsy needle must be made, until enough tissue sample for an accurate diagnosis is obtained; adjacent vascular structures’ involvement is accurately evaluated as well (T cathegory).

2.MDCECT (multidetector contrast enhanced CTscan) using thin slices is the most accurate imaging technique for assessing local extension of a pancreatic tumor (T cathegory), and for detection of liver mets (M cathegory) as well. Lymph nodes (Ncathegory) larger than 1cm are usually considered metastatic.

3.Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) – isnotcurrentlyused for diagnostic purposes nowadays, due to potential complications; thus, although it is considered too invasive as a diagnostic procedure, yet it isminimal invasive as a therapeutical one (endoscopic palliation of jaundice and duodenal stenoses).

4.Transparietohepatic cholangiography (TPC) consists of the transparietal puncture/cannulation under US or CT guidance, of a dilated bile duct (Okuda technique); advancing a cannula to the distal bile duct stenosis, then opacification of the whole intra- and extrahepatic biliary tree with contrast. It is invasive and may be used in exceptionalcases of retrograde transpapillary approach failure, as an associated procedure (guide wire introduced transhepatic downstream,grasped transpapillary and used by the endoscopist for retrograde canulation/stent insertion of bile duct stenosis – the so called “rendesvous” technique). This technique is not currently used for diagnostic as it entails complications: hemorrhage, bile leaks (choleperitoneum), bile collection. Even for therapeutical reasons, it is exceptionally used for biliary external decompression in cases in which jaundice palliation by retrograde endoscopic stenting fails and bilirubine level is very high.

5.Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI ) has a similar, yet sometimes higher, sensitivity and specificity (especially in detecting small hepatic mets) when compared with CT scan.

6.Angio-MRI, is able to detect tumoral invasion of adjacent vascular structures (portal vein, superior mesenteric artery/vein, etc), as well as vascular anatomical variants.

7.Colangio - MRI is the most accurate technique in detecting bile intraductal obstacles, especially in small tumors, suspected but not detected by other techniques; it is most valuable in establishing differential diagnosis among periampullary tumors.

8.Staging laparoscopy (SL) is very useful in detecting the so called “occult metastases” (small, millimetric peritoneal or hepatic deposits, undetectable even by the most performant CT scaners !).

  • SL issystematically indicated in all pancreatic body and tail cancers.
  • In the so called “radiologically resectable” pancreatichead carcinomas,

SL is indicated in well sellectad cases (tumors larger than 3cm, CA 19-9 exceeding 150U/ml, locally advanced tumors). In cases in which occult peritoneal carcinomatosis or liver mets (which can be harvested under direct visual control) are detected by SL, endoscopic, not surgical, palliation of jaundice and duodenal stenosis are the best options. Thus the number of useless, nontherapeutical laparotomies is dramatically reduced. Moreover, true M0 locally advanced cases will benefit of expensive and efficient palliative (or neoadjuvant) chemoradiotherapy protocols (from which disseminated-M1- cases have to be excluded). Finally, videolaparoscopy can be completed with laparoscopic ultrasonography, for a more accurate assesment of vascular peritumoral structures or small intrahepatic mets.

TREATMENT OF PANCREATIC NEOPLASM

Surgical treatment includes radical procedures, with curative intent and palliative ones. The choice of one of the above depends on thepreoperative accurate staging of the case. It has to be emphasized that at presentation, in 75% to 85% of the PHC cases, tumors are unresectable due to local extension, metastatic dissemination or both. Therefore the vast majority of patients will actually benefit only by palliative procedures.

Radical treatment:

The only chance for cure is radical surgery (R0 resection). After a thorough preoperative selection (T1, T2, T3, N0-M0, N1-M0) only 15-25% of cases become candidates for curative resection. Five years survival after an initially-considered radical surgery, is 10-25%.

For pancreatic head carcinoma,pancreaticoduodenectomy (KauschWhippeloperation) is the surgical procedure of choice, one of the most complex abdominal procedures.

Preoperative preparation of the patient prior to such a demanding surgical procedure is of paramount importance. There are some important altered biological parameters that have to be.......Patients with obstructive jaundice, especially those with........Many of these patients do not even present significant weight loss and have an apparently good physical status. Jaundice is their single complaint. Nevertheless the surgeon knows that behind this painless jaundice, important metabolic disturbances are in progress since a long time now:- malnutrition : is a direct consequence of the concomitant mechanical obstruction of both main pancreatic and main bile duct. Thus, neither the bile, nor the pancreatic juice will play their essential role any more, resulting in a severe maldigestion and malabsorbtion. Hypoalbuminaemia is one of the consequences.

Technically, removing the pancreatic head tumor, necessitates a concomitant multivisceral resection (gall bladder, main bile duct, gastric antrum, entire duodenum together with the pancreatic head, and 10-20cm from initial jejunum). Resection is followed by digestive tract reconstruction: pancreato-gastro, or pancreato-jejunal, hepatico-jejunal and gastro-jejunal anastomoses respectivelly. The weak point of this operation is the anastomosis between the pancreatic stump and the digestive tract (stomach or jejunum) often precarious due to the risk of anastomotic fistula in 6-35% of cases (with a mortality rate of 20-40%).

In well selected cases, resections can be extended to the pancreatic remnant (subtotal or total pancreatectomy) and/or to the adjacent (limited invaded) vascular structures (superior mesenteric/portal vein) in order to fulfil the main goal: R0 resection.

Regional pancreatectomy (RP), initiated in 1972 by Fortner (Mayo Clinic), is a super-radical operation. At that time Fortner extended the respectability rate from 10 to 40%, includingthe so called “iresectable”cases with posterior vascular invasion. Thus, after the segmental resection of the invaded vessels, restoration of blood flow was achieved as follows:

  • portal vein, by mesentero-portal end-to-end anastomosis (type I operation)
  • superior mesenteric artery, by reimplantation into the aorta (type II)
  • hepatic artery, by interposing a graft between it and the aorta. However,while portal vein resection is justified (no suplimentary morbidity/mortality), arterial resection, although technically feasible, is not (significant morbidity/mortality with no survival benefit)

Pylorus-preserving pancreaticoduodenectomy (PPPD),was initially described by Watson in 1940, but soon abandoned. Traverso and Longmire reintroduced this procedure in the late ‘70’s for chronic pancreatitis. Nowadays PPPD has been widely adopted as gold standard technique for resection of the periampullary tumors, including pancreatic head carcinoma, with excellent oncological results.

The main advantage of this procedure is a significant earlier postoperative weight gain and a superior alimentary confort, due to the anatomical and functional integrity of the praserved stomach.

In severelly jaundiced patients,biliary decompression is necessary before a radical operation in order to prevent a fatal postoperative acute liver failure. This may be achieved by transparietohepatic approach (external biliary drainage) or by retrograde endoscopic placement of a plastic biliary stent (internal biliary drainage) – method of choice).

Octreotide(synthetic analogue of somatostatin) may be used in order to reduce the risk of pancreatic anastomotic fistula by 40-50%. (not evidence based!).

In pancreatic body and tail tumors, distal spleno-pancreatectomy is the procedure of choice. Resectability rates and prognosis are even worse when compared with PHC.

Paliative treatment:

As resectability rates are that low, the vast majority of pancreatic cancer cases will actually benefit only by palliative procedures, having three main therapeutical targets : - jaundice

  • duodenal obstruction
  • pain.

Various surgical and nonsurgical methods are available nowadays, making it possible to adjust the propper treatment protocol to each stage of the disease, even to each specific case.

Jaundice:

Palliative surgical procedures. Surgical palliation of jaundice is usually indicated in nonmetastatic (M0), locally advanced, unresectable cases (longer estimated life expectancy of 18-24 months).As a rule, it consists of anastomoses between the distended extrahepatic bile ducts (gall baldder, ductus choledocus or ductus hepaticus) and the digestive tract (stomach, duodenum or jejunum), resulting in an efficient biliary decompression.

1- Cholecysto-duodenal or cholecysto-jejunal anastomosis: although the technique is short and symple, efficiency of the biliary drainage is limited given the early invasion by the pancreatic head tumor (2-3 months) of the choledochus and the cystico-hepatic duct junction, usually situated low, near the tumor. Nowadays it is exceptionally indicated in cases with very short live expectancy ( i. e. peritoneal carcinomatosis), in which other minimally invasive biliary drainage techniques have had failed (or are not available).

2- Choledoco-duodenostomy drains well the bile for a while, but as the tumor grows, it will be re-invaded before long (6-9 months).

3- Roux-en-Y hepatico-jejunostomy is the best technique for surgical jaundice palliation. The main bile duct is transsected up, far from the tumor, just below the hilar bifurcation and anastomosed termino-laterally to a Roux en Y jejunal loop; the biliary drainage is highly eficient and has the longest patency of all other surgical diversions; moreover, invasion of the anastomosis rarelly occures before patient’s death, as it is placed far from the growing pancreatic tumorSince it also generates bigger morbidity and even mortality it will be indicated in fit patients with longer (more than 12-18 months) life expectancy (local extended, nonmetastatic).

Duodenal stenosis/gastric outlet obstruction.

-Gastroenterostomy, in a latero-lateral manner, is a symple technical procedure that permits the gastric alimentary content to by-pass the stenotic/invaded duedenum. Finally, 7-9% of the patients with bilio-digestive diversion will require a tharepeutic gastric by-pass later.

Some authors advocate the so called prophilactic gastric by-pass, separatelly or on the same jejunal Roux en Y loop, concomitant with the biliary diversion, with no significant increase of postoperative morbidity or mortality. Yet, we consider that this procedure is unnecessary for more than 90% of the patients.

Side-to-side gastro-jejunal anastomosis may be associated if the duodenum is involved and the patients present signs of duodenal stenosis. -

  • Double biliaryand digestive diversion can be used only in well selected

cases in a prophilactic manner; yet the indication remains only for cases with initially double (biliary and duodenal concomitant stenoses) generated by unresectable, locally advancedtumors, in the absence of any detectable mathastases (T3-4, N0-2, M0).

Mean survival rate of palliative measures is 6 months (rarely 11-18 months).

After radical resections, 5 year survival is extremely rare, which shows the intention rather than claim of oncological radicality; most cases present remote metastases, impossible to catch in good time.

In order to treat pain, a major symptom in the corpus locations, chemical splanchnicectomy (preferred nowdays) is performed, consisting of the injection in the celiac plexus area of a neurolithic substance (6% phenol or 50% alcohol), with good results in 80% of the cases, through different possible approaches (open surgery, laparoscopic surgery, or during endosonography guiding, transgastric approach).

Another option for eficient pain reliev is the thoracoscopic splanchnicectomy

Radiotherapy by external or even intraoperative radiation (intraoperative), or postoperative, has not got well documented results as yet.

Chemotherapy using at least 3 agents concomitantly, has poor results so far yet some protocols tend to show promosing results.

Chemotherapy combined with radiation therapy improves survival of patients with advanced pancreatic cancer, though such methods have only recently started.

To conclude, the modest therapeutic results are due to late diagnosis of the cancer of the pancreas, even at present when the new methods may detect 1-2 cm tumors.

Further research is hoped to determine better diagnosis and more efficient therapy for this disease.

ACINAR ADENOCARCINOMA

It is a rare tumor (1% of epithelial tumors), occurring at advanced ages, and possibly reaching large sizes. It may have necrotic areas inside. Evolution is usually silent until metastases are produced.

MUCINOUS CYSTADENOMA is a large cystic tumor (2-20 cm), surrounded by a well vascularized capsule with brownish red content and numerous growths. It is more frequently located at the pancreatic corpus or tail. After removal, prognosis is good in half the cases.

INSULINOMA

It is a tumor of the beta-islet cells that secretes insulin. It occurs in patients between 40-70 years old. In most cases it is a benign insular adenoma. In 10% of the cases it may be malignant. Though it has a reduced malignancy, hypersecreting metastases may be a cause of recurrence.

Pathomorphology: macroscopically insulinoma looks like a small nodule, rather firm, located at the head or tail of the pancreas. Ectopic locations may occur in 10% of the cases (duodenal or gastric wall, spleen hilum, retroperitoneum, peritoneal flaps).

Typically, histological distinction between benign and malignant insulinomas is difficult.

Clinical picture Initially, such a case is erroneously interpreted as a neurological one, due to following types ofneuropsychiatric manifestations:

-central nervous: diplopia, convulsions, coma

-sympathetic nervous system: flushing, sweating, vomiting, persistent hunger

-psychiatric: restlessness, mental instability, disorientation.

Later on, the clinician will find out that all these signs and symptoms recurr at regular intervals in association with periodical bouts of hypoglycemia, due to excessive insulin release (after physical exercise or prolonged fasting) and subside postprandially (especially after eating sweeets). Thus, clinical diagnosis is based on the famous Whippletriad:

1 - insulin shock (hypoglycemia) induced by exercise or fasting

2 - low glycemia – under 50 mg% - during bouts

3 - symptoms subside after glucose administration.

Evolution of this condition is oscillating, as acute attacks are followed by variable remissions. There are mild variants, with spontaneous remission, or severe, potentially fatal ones, if emergency treatment is not promptly initiated.

Laboratory findings:

1. Glycemia: after prolonged fasting, during crisis or after

exercise, decrease below 40mg% is suggestive.

2. Insulinemia, determined by radioimmunoassay, is increased.

Values over 6 UI/ml correlated with low glycemia.

3. Proinsulinemia, determined by radioimmunoassay, is highly

specific, being also a marker of malignancy.

4. Ratio between serum insulin/blood glucose concentrations is

close to 1.0 (in patients whithout insulinoma, this ratio is 0.3-0.4).

5. Secretin stimulation test: intravenous administration of

secretin will result, in normal subjects, insignificant increase of

insulin levels, which is not the case with cases with insulinoma.

Imaging findings:

1. Ultraosnography; generally, the appearance of an insulinoma at US examination is as a hypoechoic lesion with clear margins.

  • Percutaneous abdominal US has an accuracy of 50-60% in detecting

insulinomas.

  • Endoscopic US, has a better accuracy, being able to detect smaller

tumors (transducer endoscopically placed in the close vicinity of tumor).

  • Intraoperative US,is used in association with the surgeon’s palpation in

cases with small tumors, suspected but not detected before operation.

  • Laparoscopic US is a promising imaging technique; it is used in cases

in which excision is planned to be performed by this approach (enucleation or central pancreatectomy).

2. Computed tomography: has a better accuracy. As insulinomas are hypervascular tumors, they appear as low density tumors in plain CT.

3. Magnetic resonance imaging: it’s accuracy might be as high as 85%; it offers important informations concerninginternal features of the tumor.

Sensitivity of US, CT and MRI imaging techniques increases with the size of the tumor.

4. Selective celiac angiography has the highest diagnostic accuracy (6080%), followed by CT and US as sensitivity.

Treatment

  • Radical treatment is onlysurgical excision; itleads to cure in most cases

(75-80%).

A minute surgical exploration of the whole pancreas and organs that may include ectopic locations should be performed.

Intraoperative ultrasound is extremely useful, as it may identify small, unsuspected tumors.

  • Unique, superficial, well encapsulated and delimited tumors may be

enucleated.

  • Tumors located deep in the corpus or tail of the gland, need to be excised

“en block”by a corporeo-caudal pancreatectomy, by open or laparoscopic approach.

  • In selected cases (benign tumors), central pancreatectomy might be a

good option (it preserves the pancreatic head,partially the body together with the tail of the gland; in this technique, the spleen is preserved as well.

  • Tumors located in the pancreatic headrequire pancreaticoduodenectomy

(Whipple procedure).

Radicality of tumor resection is evaluated intraoperativelly by measuring plasma insulin levels, before and after excision !

Due to difficult histologic differentiation between benign and malignant insulinomas, although reccurence rate is low, sometimes, malignancy can be affirmed only after occurance of matastases.

  • In malignant insulinomas with liver metastases, embolization of the

hepatic artery is performed.

  • - Conservative treatment consists of raising blood glucose levels using

insulin antagonists (Diazoxid - it inhibits releasing of insulin from the tumor)

  • in cases of frequent and severe attacks -or suppressors of pancreatic

secretion (somatostatin).

Chemotherapy, indicated for inoperable malignant insulinomas using multiple chemotherapy agents, might have good results as well.

GLUCAGONOMA

It is a rare pancreatic tumor affecting mainly women (8/1 gender ratio) in their 6th decade of life.

Pathomorphology: the tumor is commonly located in the pancreatic body or tail (60%), extended to the whole organ (30%), orlimited at the head of the gland ( 10%). It often becomes malignant. Tumor originates in the glucagon secreting alpha cells.

Most of glucagonomas are malignant and voluminous when diagnosed.

Clinical features include: -cutaneous lesions such as migratory necrotising erythema ( it is devolping in 7-14 days, starting from maculas, pustules containing often infected fluid, that break and ganerate crusts; the area remains pigmented). Most frequent locations are the perineal and buttocks areas, extremities, front chest. Glossitis, mouth corner sores and vulvovaginitis may occur as well.

-Diabetes mellitus is the second clinical element with benign evolution,

easy to balance.

-Anemia occurs due to low nutritional supply (anorexia) and

hypoaminoacidemia.

-Body weight loss is due to poor feeding and antianabolic action of

glucagons.

-Deep vein thrombosis.

Laboratory findings:

-Radioimmune dosage of serum glucagon (levels over 500 pg/ml) confirms the diagnosis based on the clinical picture.

Imaging diagnosis: ultrasound examination (percutaneous, endoscopic, intraoperativelly or laparoscopic) and CT usually identify the tumor. Preoperative histological diagnosis may be performed by US (best by endoscopic US)- guided biopsy.

In case of doubt, hyperglycemia challenge test with exogenous glucagons may be performed.

Differential diagnosis is made with primary diabetes mellitus with eczematous skin lesions. Serum glucagon levels increase in other diseases as well (liver cirrhosis, chronic pancreatitis, Cushing’s syndrome), but never over 500 pg/ml !

Treatment: Tipically, although low growing, gastrinomas are usually diagnosed in advanced stages, as voluminous, locally extended tumors. Yet, as the only hope for cure is surgical resection, tumor ablation is performed even in the presence of metastases, in which case associated polychemotherapy offers longer survival.

Palliative debulking excisions may, due to important consecutive decrease in glucagon serum levels, alleviate symptoms.

Repeated multiple re-excisions for local or metastatic recurrences can significantly prolong survival and improve quality of patients’ lives.

Even hepatic transplantations for liver metastatic disease(isolated cases) have been reported.

GASTRINOMA

Pancreatic tumor secreting gastrin, determining hypersecretion of HCl in the stomach, responsible for gastric and duodenal ulcers, frequently multiple, refractory to treatment, a syndrome described by Zollinger-Ellison.

Pathomorphology – according to location, gastrinomas are of two categories:

  • eutopic, in areas normally containing G cells that secrete gastrin

(antrum, duodenal bulb, jejunum)

  • ectopic, in areas usually not containing G cells (pancreas,

mesenteric ganglia, ovary, spleen hilum).

Gastrinomas are often multiple (80%) and malignant (2/3 of cases),

especially the ectopic ones; however, the degree of malignancy is low.

Clinical and biological classification

  • Type I – solitary up to 50% of the cases, mostly eutopic,

malignancy in 60-90% of cases;

  • - Type II – multiple small tumors located in the pancreas, mostly

benign

Clinical pictureis of multiple gastric, duodenal, jejunal ulcers, refractory to treatment, entailing many complications, maximal acid hypersecretion not influenced by treatment, diarrhea and steatorrhea due to the large volume of gastric acid secretion.

The phenomena are due to gastrin-like G-17 and G-34 substances in the circulation, with great molecular weight, that permanently stimulate the acid-secreting cells in the stomach.

Paraclinical examinations evidence acid hypersecretion, over 100 ml/h, baseline acid output greater than 15 mEq/h, with a ratio between baseline and maximal outputs over 0.6. Nocturnal acid volume secretion is over 21.

Basal gastrinemia is constant, 10 times the normal (over 1000 pg/ml).

Imaging techniques. Barium enema and fibroscopy of stomach and duodenum evidence the ulcers and the massive acid secretion. US, CT and selective angiography may locate the tumor. Ultrasonography performed before and during the operation has increased the possibility to detect small tumors.

Evolution: gastrinomas are usually malignant, multiple, frequently with metastases at the time of diagnosis.

Treatment: suppression of acid secretion may be achieved with high doses of H2 receptors blockers (cimetidine, ranitidine, famotidine), or omeprazol.

Somatostatin analogs efficiently inhibit hormonal and gastric secretion (ocreotide).

Surgery targeting the organ (ulcers) was the only solution until recently (total gastrectomy) is less and less applied. Vagotomy may be useful when omeprazol is not accessible or when the gastrinoma cannot be located.

The treatment of gastrinoma as such is enucleation when at the head, and corpo-caudal pancreatectomy for the respective locations.

VIPOMA

A pancreatic tumor originating in the insular non-beta cells that secrete the vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) and responsible for the VernerMorrison syndrome, characterized by watery diarrhea, hypokaliemia, hypochlorhydria, severe dehydration involving a high fatal risk.

Pathomorphology. Pancreatic VIPoma is represnted by the adenoma (43%), carcinoma (37%) or microadenomatosis of insular non-beta cells.

The clinical picture consists of numerous clinical manifestation: diarrhea (over 700 ml/24h, sometimes even 17-20 l/24h) leading to severe dehydration with hypokaliemia, metabolic acidosis, hypomagnesemia (causing tetany), hypokalemic nephropathy with uremia, extreme physical fatigue, itchy rashes, heart disturbances (rhythm, failure).

The clinical manifestations are due to the hypersecretion of VIP, which normally acts on the enterocyte inducing an active anionic secretion of chlorine and bicarbonate at the level of the small bowel, by activation of adenylcyclase. The resulting intestinal hypersecretion exceeds the colon absorption capacity and causes watery diarrhea (also called pancreatic cholera). Severe hypovolemia and hypokaliemia are the direct results. Over 20 times more kalium than by physiological processed is lost in the stool. Bicarbonate depletion leads to metabolic acidosis.

Hypo-achlorhydria is present, VIP being a strong inhibitor of acid gastric secretion.

Glucose regulation disturbances (glucose intolerance) are due to the glucogenolithic effect of VIP.

Paraclinical diagnosis. Radioimmunoassay evidences increased VIP plasma concentrations (>500 pmol/l).

Location of the tumor is achieved by US or CT scan, selective angiography being useful due to the rich vascularization of the tumor.

Treatment is surgical and consists in tumor removal. Prognosis is good in benign forms. Malignant forms are severe, survival not exceeding one year.

The most common locations, to the corpus and tail, benefit from corpocaudal pancreatectomy.

Medical treatment consists of hydroelectrolithic rebalancing, administration of somatostatin analogs (Ocretotid, Sandostatin), which can control the secretory diarrhea associated with the VIPoma.

SOMATOSTATINOMA

A rare tumor (43 case until 1990) predominating in women, maximum incidence around 32-45 years. Somatostatin secreted in excess triggers a clinical picture of biliary lithiasis, diabetes mellitus, diarrhea and statorrhea.

Pathomorphology.the tumor is located mostly to the head of the pancreas, reaching 10 cm. It has a high malignancy potential, with early metastases. Histologically it is a trabecular or glandular carcinoma of endocrine origin.

Clinical picture is determined by the pharmacological action of somatostatin: inhibits the somatotropic hormone, TSH, insulin, glucagons, gastrin, and cholecystokininpancreazimine secretions.

Diabetes mellitus is mild and not complicated.

Biliary lithiasis is due to decreased lipid absorption and gallbladder atonia.

Diarrhea with steatorrhea is present in 80% of the patients.

Nausea, vomiting, bloating, weight loss may be associated.

Paraclinical examinations, US and CT establish the tumor diagnosis. Preoperative histological diagnosis is based on US or CT-guided puncture biopsy.

Treatment is surgical according to location. Cephalic duodenopancreatectomy or corpo-caudal pancreatectomy are performed, but results are poor due to increased malignancy.

Chemotherapy also has poorer results than in the other endocrine tumors.

PANCREATIC POLYPEPTIDE (PP) SECRETING TUMOR

It accors equally in the women and men, mainly at the age of 50-55.

Pathomorphology; location to the pancreatic head is more common.

Clinical picture is not specific, consisting of diarrhea with or without steatorrhea, basal hypochlorhydria, weight loss, due to the PP inhibitory effect of gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion.

Paraclinical examination: radioimmunoassay evidences high PP plasma concentration (over 1000 pg/ml).

Imaging techniques: CT scan, pre- and intraoperative US establish the tumor location.

Treatmentconsists of the tumor removal based on the same principles as for pancreatic adenocarcinoma.

Therapy with streptozocin or somatostatin analogs may be associated.

CARCINOID TUMOR

It has a rare location in the pancreas, originating in the isles, in the chromaffin cells.

Symptomatology is not specific. Due to 5-hydroxytriptophane and sertotonin secretion:- flushing may occur

  • arterial hypertension
  • oedema around the eyes
  • hypersecretion of saliva and tears
  • diarrhea, abdominal pain, all these phenomena occurring in paroxistic

bouts. It has a high malignancy potential.

Current imaging techniques identify the tumor.

Treatmentis surgical and is represented by pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure). The results are similar to pancreatic adenocarcinoma, namely modest.
